text: The impresario had fixed forty days as the longest period of fasting, beyond which he would never allow it to continue, not even in the great cities, and he had good reason for this limit. <break time="0.8s" /> Experience had shown that for about forty days the publics interest could be stirred up by steadily increasing advertising, but after that it began to fade, and a clear decline in attendance could be observed. <break time="0.8s" /> So on the fortieth day the door of the flower decked cage was opened, a military band played, and two doctors entered the cage to take the necessary measurements, the results of which were announced through a megaphone. <break time="0.8s" /> Then two young ladies, delighted to have been chosen for the honor, came to lead him out of the cage and down a few steps to a small table on which a light meal for invalids was waiting. <break time="0.8s" /> At this moment, however, the hunger artist always resisted, and although he willingly laid his bony arms in the ladies helpful hands, he refused to stand up, asking himself why he should stop now, after only forty days. <break time="0.8s" /> He could have held out longer, so why should he be robbed of the glory of not merely being the greatest hunger artist of all time, a title he had perhaps already earned, but of surpassing even himself. <break time="0.8s" /> Then the impresario stepped forward and lifted his arms over the artist, as though inviting heaven itself to admire this pitiful martyr on the straw, and a martyr he truly was, though in an entirely different sense. <break time="0.8s" /> Gripping the frail waist with exaggerated care, he handed the artist over to the pale ladies, and while a meal was fed into the half fainting man, the impresario chatted cheerfully to keep the audience from noticing his condition.
